strengths: Novel capability for incremental 3D avatar reconstruction with variable-length inputs, enabling flexible data utilization that existing methods (LAM single-frame, Avat3r fixed 4-frame) cannot achieve
Unified framework handling diverse scenarios (monocular images, multi-view, video) within a single model, more practical than separate specialized models

Comprehensive and convincing experimental validation: consistent improvements over multiple baselines across 1-16 input views, multiple datasets (NeRSemble, Ava256, INSTA), with both quantitative metrics and qualitative results
Well-motivated technical design with multi-granular guidance encoding (camera, expression, head pose) specifically tailored for 3D avatar reconstruction, demonstrating thoughtful problem formulation
Thorough ablation studies (Table 2) validating each component's contribution, wide-range viewpoint generalization tests, and FLAME robustness analysis
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, implementation details in appendix, promise to release code, and comprehensive supplementary materials
Fast reconstruction speed (1.33-26.06s for 1-16 frames) with competitive rendering performance (17-240 FPS) while maintaining quality, addressing practical deployment concerns
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: architecture heavily builds on existing VGGT framework with relatively straightforward modifications (replacing DPT with MLP, adding pose/expression encodings); core losses are standard (L1 landmark supervision, photometric losses)

Fundamental expressiveness limitations from FLAME dependency: cannot reconstruct structures outside FLAME topology (tongue, complex muscle dynamics), struggles with fine-grained details (wrinkles, eye-gaze), limiting real-world applicability despite being acknowledged

Insufficient justification for design choices: no analysis of why VGGT is the right architecture, why dual-stream DiT blocks specifically, sensitivity to loss weights (hand-tuned λ values), or how Nsliced was selected; 68 landmarks seem sparse for supervising millions of Gaussian parameters

Experimental design concerns: LAM modified for fair multi-frame comparison but this change affects its original single-image design; Avat3r comparison uses only published results; large ablation impact of Global Attention (L1 increases 2.4x) not deeply analyzed

Incremental reconstruction evaluation incomplete: while Figures 4-5 demonstrate improvement, quantitative analysis of marginal gains per additional frame is limited; streaming reconstruction shown but not thoroughly evaluated or analyzed

Generalization concerns: trained exclusively on 12-camera NeRSemble setup with limited background variation; robustness to diverse lighting, makeup, accessories, and real-world capture conditions not systematically evaluated

Insufficient analysis of failure modes and robustness: FLAME tracking noise tested (Table 4) but other failure modes not analyzed; no user studies for perceptual quality; identity metric (ArcFace) is coarse without fine-grained facial attribute evaluation

High computational cost: training requires 8 H100 GPUs for 14 days; inference on 48GB RTX 4090 not broadly accessible; scalability to smaller hardware and memory consumption issues during training not discussed

Missing comparisons and depth: limited evaluation against recent 2025 methods (e.g., LHM not compared); no animation quality evaluation; some design choices (e.g., why 504×504 resolution, why specific layer counts) lack justification

strengths: Clear problem motivation: Identifies genuine limitations of existing methods (fixed-length inputs, poor sparse data handling, low data utilization efficiency) that affect practical deployment
Novel incremental reconstruction paradigm: Enables progressive quality improvement with additional frames, genuinely useful for real-world scenarios where data arrives asynchronously

Comprehensive experimental validation: Systematic evaluation across 1/4/8/16 input views, multiple datasets (NeRSemble, Ava256, INSTA), appropriate metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, ArcFace identity), and thorough ablation studies (Table 2)
Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements across all configurations (e.g., PSNR +2.78 over LAM at 1 view, LPIPS +0.110 at 4 views) with identity preservation gains (0.116 vs 0.135 at 1 view)
Practical unified framework: Single model handles diverse real-world inputs (single image, monocular video, multi-view) without requiring separate variants, addressing real usability concern

Well-designed technical components: Multi-granular guidance encoding (camera, expression, pose) is sensible for diverse inputs; landmark tracking and sliced fusion losses effectively enable aggregation
Reproducibility efforts: Provides detailed hyperparameters, training procedures, data preparation details, robustness analysis (Table 4), and promises code release
Clear presentation: Well-organized paper with effective motivation, good use of figures to explain approach, comprehensive related work grounding
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: LGRT is explicitly a variant of VGGT with main modifications being DPT→MLP replacement and FLAME vertex prompts; these are incremental changes rather than novel innovations

Critical FLAME dependency: Heavy reliance on FLAME tracking for pose/expression estimation significantly constrains generalization; acknowledged inability to represent fine-grained muscle dynamics, eye-gaze, or out-of-FLAME structures (tongue) limits representation capacity

Overclaimed incremental reconstruction: Still requires 16 base frames for reasonable quality; additional frames require full model reprocessing (not constant-time); FramePack strategy (C.3) feels ad-hoc; Figure 5 shows quality plateaus significantly beyond 16 frames, questioning streaming utility

Comparison fairness concerns: LAM* is a modified version enabling multi-frame fusion (potentially not reflecting original design); Avat3r comparison relies on published results only; missing direct comparisons with recent 2025 methods (Arc2Avatar, HeadGap, GPAvatar)

Insufficient technical justification: No analysis of why 16 base frames are optimal, why specific attention interleaving is better, or rationale for loss weights (λ values appear arbitrary); limited investigation of why optimization methods fail beyond data scarcity

Limited generalization analysis: Training on NeRSemble with 12 controlled camera views; Ava256 evaluation uses FLAME tracking from images; generalization to diverse capture conditions (lighting, resolution, quality) not thoroughly explored

Evaluation limitations: No user studies or perceptual evaluations; proxy metrics (PSNR/SSIM) don't always correlate with perceptual quality; ArcFace identity metric is limited; no quantitative pose/expression accuracy evaluation; failure case analysis is superficial

Incremental computational cost: Modeling time scales with frames (1.33s→26.06s); not truly constant-time incremental updates; training requires 8 H100 GPUs for 14 days, high computational barrier to reproducibility
Missing ablations: No sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters (attention layers, hidden dimensions, loss balance); no comparison of alternative attention interleaving patterns

Presentation issues: Some overclaiming ('pioneering incremental 3D avatar reconstruction'); Figure 2 appears twice; notation inconsistencies (g, g_i, g_f, g^e_i); important details (FramePack, FLAME robustness) relegated to appendix
